name: Loss aversion
statement: Losses are said to weigh about twice as much as equal-sized gains, so a coin-flip bet needs a prize roughly double the stake before people will take it.
meaning: The claim has a number attached to it, which is unusual for a cognitive bias and is the reason it can be argued about precisely. In prospect theory the value function bends at a reference point and is steeper below it than above, and the ratio of the two slopes is a parameter, lambda. A lambda of 2 means a person is indifferent between a coin flip that wins £20 and loses £10, and taking nothing. Lambda of 1 means gains and losses carry the same weight. Two things follow that are often run together. One is a claim about risky choice, which is what lambda measures. The other is a family of riskless phenomena, the endowment effect and status quo bias, which loss aversion is used to explain and which are then cited back as evidence for it. Risk aversion is a third thing again. Turning down a fair coin flip follows from the diminishing marginal utility of wealth with no kink at the reference point, and Gal and Rucker hold that where large amounts of money are involved loss aversion cannot be told apart from risk aversion over changes in wealth.

origin.note: "Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk" introduced the kinked value function, steeper for losses than for gains. The familiar coefficient came thirteen years later, from Tversky and Kahneman's 1992 paper in the Journal of Risk and Uncertainty, which reports lambda = 2.25. Walasek, Mullett and Stewart describe that estimate as one of the first attempts to fit lambda. It came from 25 graduate students in one-hour sessions, choosing between hypothetical lotteries and sums of money for certain. They also report that of the prospects used, 28 were pure gains, 28 pure losses and eight mixed, and only the eight mixed ones bear on lambda. The 1992 paper is paywalled and no open copy was located during this check, so its sample and design are attributed to them rather than read off the original.

evidence: Three separate bodies of work sit under the one name. In risky choice, lambda is fitted to accept-or-reject decisions over 50-50 gambles mixing a gain and a loss. Stake size moves the result. Ert and Erev put the same bet to 46 undergraduates for real money at two magnitudes. An even chance of winning or losing 100 Sheqels drew 22 percent takers, well below half at p < .001. The same bet at 10 Sheqels drew 48 percent, which is chance. In riskless choice, Kahneman, Knetsch and Thaler reported that sellers of a university mug demanded more than buyers would pay. That is the endowment effect. Samuelson and Zeckhauser reported a preference for whichever option was labelled current, the status quo bias. Xiao, Lam, Piara and Feldman replicated that paper twice on Mechanical Turk, both runs preregistered, with 311 and 316 participants. They found the bias in three of its four scenarios, with the smallest odds ratio in the first scenario at 2.47, 95% CI [1.37, 4.44], and no support in the wagon-colour scenario. In the field, Pope and Schweitzer analysed over 2.5 million putts on the PGA Tour with laser measurements. Professionals, Tiger Woods included, putt better for par than for birdie from the same distance. They read that as loss aversion around the reference point of par.

examples.text: A colleague offers to toss a coin for £50. Almost nobody accepts, and many still refuse when the prize is raised to £80 against the same £50 stake. The refusal prices a loss above a gain of the same size, which is what the ratio is meant to measure.

A scheme pays £2,000 for a good quarter and deducts £1,000 for a bad one. Staff treat the deduction as the larger number and play safe, although the arithmetic favours taking the chance. The asymmetry sits in the weighting rather than in the odds.

examples.tag: The side protecting a one-goal lead
examples.text: A team a goal ahead with twenty minutes left drops deep instead of pressing for a second. Conceding is felt as worse than scoring is felt as good, so two outcomes of the same size are not treated as the same size.

replication.headline: Two meta-analyses published in the same year put the coefficient at 1.96 and at 1.31, and a re-analysis finds the higher figure comes from gambles where the losses on offer were smaller than the gains.
replication.detail: Brown, Imai, Vieider and Camerer pooled 607 estimates from 150 articles published between 1992 and 2017 and report a mean coefficient of 1.955, with 95 percent probability that the true value lies in [1.820, 2.102]. Walasek, Mullett and Stewart took only studies where prospect theory could be fitted to individual choices between mixed gambles. They found 19 usable datasets from 17 articles and report 1.31, 95% CI [1.10, 1.53], an interval that excludes 2.25. Twelve of the 19 datasets had intervals covering loss neutrality and six had intervals covering 2.25. Yechiam and Zeif then re-analysed Brown and colleagues' own dataset. They sorted 163 estimates from 84 papers, covering 149,218 participants, by whether losses matched gains in size and whether the gambles were shown in order of size. The pooled result comes back at 1.82, 95% CI [1.73, 1.91]. Within it the modal design, smaller losses than gains and ordered presentation, gives a median of 2.295 across 62 estimates. The 22 estimates using symmetric gains and losses in no particular order, from 1,985 participants, give 1.07, 95% CI [0.97, 1.18], which is not distinguishable from loss neutrality (Z = 1.39, p = .16). Walasek and Stewart had shown the same dependence experimentally in 2015. Among 323 analysed participants on Mechanical Turk, gains up to $40 against losses up to $20 gave a median lambda of 1.79, 95% CI [1.55, 2.00]. Symmetric $20 ranges gave 1.00, 95% CI [0.99, 1.01]. Reversing the ranges gave 0.88, 95% CI [0.81, 1.00], the opposite of loss aversion. The defence is not empty. Mrkva, Johnson, Gächter and Herrmann tested moderators across five samples totalling 17,720 people, found that knowledge and experience lower loss aversion, and report that people at every level of both were loss averse. They also reject the claim that loss aversion is fully explained by status quo bias, by risk aversion, or by the educated laboratory samples the field usually recruits. Zeif and Yechiam re-ran that paradigm and replicated it as published. Then they removed the asymmetric amounts and the ordering. Across five studies with 2,001 participants they found no loss aversion for small sums, a mean lambda of 1.16 at average losses of $40, and 1.54 at $100. Bleichrodt and L'Haridon ran the test from the other direction. They measured 266 students at the Erasmus School of Economics, 242 of whom were analysed, with the high-stakes payoffs set at 200 times the small ones. Median coefficients across eight conditions ran from 1.24 to 1.46, each above 1 at p < 0.01, and the small-stakes and high-stakes figures did not differ, all p > 0.38.

study.cite: Yechiam, E., & Zeif, D. (2025). Loss aversion is not robust: A re-meta-analysis. Journal of Economic Psychology, 107, 102801.

limits: One preregistered multi-country replication sits beside this work, and it does not measure lambda. Ruggeri and colleagues re-ran 17 of the 20 items from the 1979 paper with 4,098 participants in 19 countries and 13 languages. Ninety-four percent of items replicated, and 12 of the 13 theoretical contrasts, ten of those in every country. All three of the contrasts that varied by country tested the reflection effect. The items are gain-only or loss-only prospects for hypothetical money rather than the mixed gambles lambda is fitted from, and the authors put their result as upholding the 1979 conclusions and, in their words, 'by default, some principles of loss aversion'. Searches of Crossref, PubMed, Europe PMC and the journals themselves located no Many Labs or Registered Replication Report entry for the loss-aversion coefficient itself. The rest of the record consists of meta-analyses, re-analyses of those meta-analyses, and single-laboratory experiments. That matters because every number above is a model fit rather than a measurement, and the models disagree. André and de Langhe hold that the 2015 reversal disappears when lambda is estimated only on the gambles common to every condition. Walasek, Mullett and Stewart concede the point in their 2021 reply, agreeing that comparing lambda across conditions was problematic, and argue the flaw is wider: lambda estimated from accept-or-reject tasks is too noisy to rank the same people consistently across random splits of their own data. That cuts against their 1.31 as much as against 2.25. The cell carrying the sceptical case in Yechiam and Zeif rests on 22 estimates and about 2,000 participants out of 149,218. Their trim-and-fill correction moves it to 0.94, which they advise reading with caution because the rank-correlation test was not significant. Bleichrodt and L'Haridon make the deeper objection to the sceptics: the behavioural definition of loss aversion the small-stakes results rely on comes from the 1979 theory, and under the 1992 version it confounds the kink at the reference point with diminishing sensitivity and probability weighting. Their own experiment did not play the loss questions for real. Yechiam's review of the pre-1979 utility studies concluded that very large losses were overweighted while smaller ones often were not, and Ert and Erev found the same pattern with real money. Bleichrodt and L'Haridon, controlling for the confounds, found no reliable stake-size effect. Whether lambda rises with stake size is therefore itself unsettled.
misreadings: The most common error is treating one number as three findings. Loss aversion in risky choice, the endowment effect and status quo bias are distinct claims with distinct evidence, and support for one is routinely reported as support for the others. Zeif and Yechiam found only a weak correlation between the endowment effect and loss aversion in the same participants, with the endowment effect present where loss aversion was absent. Gal and Rucker's review makes the sharper version of the objection. In the standard endowment and status quo procedures, keeping is also the inaction option, so loss and gain are confounded with doing nothing and doing something. When they decoupled the two, willingness to pay to retain a good stopped exceeding willingness to pay to obtain it, and for fibre-optic internet service the obtain figure was higher, $50.43 against $43.75. Simonson and Kivetz reply in the same issue that the conclusion is overstated, while granting that loss aversion is less robust and universal than has been assumed. Their proposal is to treat it as contingent on moderators rather than true until disproved. The second error is quoting 2.25 as a constant of human nature. It is a median from one small study of hypothetical choices in 1992, and the coefficient recovered from a given experiment tracks the range of amounts that experiment happened to show. The third is enrolling the sunk-cost effect as evidence. Gal and Rucker note that it compares no gain with any loss and so cannot speak to the ratio, and they put the disposition effect in the same class. A fourth is treating any preference for the status quo as loss aversion. Gal and Rucker quote Kahneman's own position that swapping essentially identical goods is not coded as loss and gain, then offered 149 Mechanical Turk participants a $20 bill in exchange for another $20 bill and still found a clear preference for keeping the original.
